motion: I THEREFORE MOVE that the City Council INSTRUCT the City Administrative Officer, with assistance from the Bureau of Street Lighting, to report back in 30 days with options identifying $6.6 M for immediate use by BSL to maintain workforce and baseline services, including feasibility of repurposing MICLA funding previously approved for use by the BSL by the City Council and Mayor. The results were presented to Council on June 26 and unfortunately District NO. 5500 failed to pass. In response to ramifications of the failed vote, the Council directed BSL, with the assistance from the City Attorney’s Office, City Administrative Officer, the Chief Legislative Analyst, and any additional necessary departments, to present recommendations on how to mitigate immediate impacts to lighting services, update BSL fees to ensure full cost recovery, and options to monetize BSL’s existing assets. This report answers both CF 26-0955 and 25-0600-S109: Revenue Generating Opportunities for the Bureau of Street Lighting. FISCAL SITUATION OF BSL At the start of FY26/27 the Bureau faces immediate fiscal challenges. As a result of reductions to the Bureau’s hiring hall funding in the FY 26-27 budget and no current interim transfers to absorb the additional costs, the Bureau risks losing approximately 15% of its field staff which amounts to 27 hiring hall positions. In addition, overtime resources are significantly constrained, as overtime was also reduced by $1M in the FY 26-27 budget through reduction exercises. The Bureau has started the fiscal year off with just $171K in adopted overtime, which puts the funding at a level that has not been seen for over 20 years, and constrains overtime use to the AN EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY EMPLOYER Recyclable and made from recycled waste. 1 most extreme emergency cases. For comparison, the Bureau easily spends $35,000 to $40,000 in overtime over a weekend fully staffed for vandalism repairs. To address the immediate funding impacts of the current budget, the Bureau recommends the following allocation of funds to restore all hiring hall positions and the operating supplies and the materials accompanying those positions, as well as the overtime lost for FY 26-27 in CWPT Fortification and the Assistant Street Lighting Electrician which was also lost from that program. documents.excerpt: Bureau of Street Lighting 1 Overview of CF 26-0955 and BSL after District No.5500 (Assessment Ballot Vote) v.261013 1 “Vermonica” x Sheila Klein Photo: Ian Byers-Gamber Bureau of Street Lighting Mission To Light the way for Los Angeles Strategic Planning & Execution Vision We build, operate, and maintain world-class systems that deliver Results and Feedback limitless beneﬁts to our neighborhoods Values People Integrity Innovation Performance Tools Community Hiring Training Ethical Codes Form 700 Policy Feedback Pilot Projects Innovation Fund Annual Reviews Goal Setting Metrics Recruiting Ordinances / Laws Technology adoption Check-ins All Staff Directives Operational meetings Project management Mentoring Reports Initiatives (e.g.: Asset Protection) Mayor / City Goals 2 CF: Verbal; 25-1510; 26-0955 The Assessment: what happens now? Because District No.5500 (the Citywide Assessment Ballot) failed to pass, BSL will operate based on the existing assessment on properties. BSL’s O&M is primarily funded by an Assessment which generates ~$45M annually since 1996, as 90% of revenues are frozen. A third party validated BSL’s estimated operational need of $125M. The oﬃcial repair times stand at 1 year+. BSL’s Assessment is based on the special beneﬁt of an improvement to a given property, calculated via land use and acreage, and collected annually via County Property Taxes. BSL levies the assessment through its powers given in City Charter, State Constitution, and the Improvement Act of 1911. In BSL’s early history (circa 1920’s), streetlights (improvements) were tied to developments using these powers. This structure and practice persists today and is why Property Owners pay for streetlights. The General Fund DOES NOT directly pay for streetlights (with many caveats). The Assessment CANNOT pay for anything other than streetlights. To change how BSL is funded would require a decision of the City and likely an electorate vote to determine funding. Governed by Prop. 218, an Assessment is established or changed through a ballot vote of affected Property Owners. It is an off-cycle protest vote (NOT electorate vote) and requires 50%+1 by weighted value of Assessment of affected Property Owners to vote yes. 3 Assessment Results by Property Type and Ownership Property Type Total Assessment Value Total Voting Value Turnout Rate "Yes" Vote $ Amount Share of Total $ Amount Share of Total (by assessment Result value) (by assessment value) Single Family Res / Condo $51,116,993 45.7% $14,544,827 38.2% 28.5% 18.1% Owner-Occupied $37,260,570 33.3% $10,289,514 27.0% 27.6% 19.3% In City of LA Owner $6,280,386 5.6% $2,009,976 5.3% 32.0% 12.2% CA Owner $6,284,035 5.6% $1,952,389 5.1% 31.1% 14.1% Out of State $1,216,660 1.1% $241,321 0.6% 19.8% 26.4% Rental Income (Apts) $28,202,309 25.2% $10,728,144 28.2% 38.0% 5.6% In City of LA Owner $17,895,060 16.0% $6,725,193 17.7% 37.6% 5.8% CA Owner $9,248,499 8.3% $3,646,909 9.6% 39.4% 5.4% Out of State $1,043,233 0.9% $353,247 0.9% 3
